newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, China leaders to meet for talks in Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China leaders to meet for talks in Moscow.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and the Chinese leader Jiang Zemin are expected crown their talks on Wednesday by signing a political declaration outlining their joint vision of the world order in the next century.

Moscow, deeply unhappy about NATO's plans to expand eastward and jealous of the claims by the United States for a leading role in the post-Cold War world, gave a warm welcome to Jiang who arrived in Moscow on Tuesday to start his five-day visit.

Yeltsin interrupted his holiday at the Black Sea resort of Sochi and arrived in Moscow on Tuesday to take part in a formal welcome for Jiang, scheduled for 10 a.m. (0600 GMT) on Wednesday, followed by talks and signing the joint declaration.

Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Monday that the declaration included a clause in which Beijing and Moscow would express their opposition to "claims by any country to the role of absolute leader." He named no state.
Moscow and Beijing have made clear they want to set an example for other countries on how to maintain security and build bilateral ties.

"This new type of relationship includes a refusal to take part in military blocs, ruling out confrontation and any menace to third parties," Interfax news agency quoted the Chinese ambassador to Moscow, Li Fenglin, as saying on Tuesday.
Jiang, Yeltsin and the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will on Thursday sign a treaty on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border.

Few details of the treaty have been made public. Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev's spokesman said on Tuesday that the five states would reduce their forces deployed near the border and pull them back 100 km (60 miles).

Yeltsin and Jiang will meet for more talks on Thursday. The Chinese leader will also meet heads of both chambers of the Russian parliament on Wednesday and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Thursday.
Jiang is also expected to address the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on Wednesday.
But Russian officials said that the declaration and the treaty were the key points of the visit.
"The fact that there are few documents on the agenda highlights the importance of each of them," a Foreign ministry official told Reuters.
"One reason keeping the agenda tight was to focus attention on the milestone quality of the issues that were included," he added.
Moscow did much to underline the importance of Jiang's visit.
The Chinese leader, accompanied by his wife Wang Yeping, will stay in the Kremlin during the visit -- a rare honour.

Jiang, who knows Russia's language and literature, will go on Friday to Yasnaya Polyana, the estate of writer and philosopher Leo Tolstoy about 200 km (130 miles) south of Moscow. He will leave Moscow on Saturday.

Apart from political benefits of rapprochement with Beijing -- with which a strong alliance in 1950s was followed by bitter rivalry in the 1960s and '70s for the leadership of world communism -- Moscow also hopes for a greater access to the Chinese market and to markets in South East Asia and the Pacific Rim.

Tass news agency said two-way trade reached $6.9 billion in 1996, 25 percent up on 1995. Russian officials have said that trade turnover could reach $8-10 billion in 1997 and $20 billion by the end of the century.
